top.name: Calgary Tower
top.what: The 191 m tower from 1968, with an observation deck, a glass floor and a view to the Rockies on a clear day.

top.name: Glenbow at the JR Shaw Centre for Arts & Culture
top.what: Western Canada's largest museum, closed for its rebuild and reopening in 2027 with general admission paid for by an endowment, so visitors pay nothing to walk in.

top.name: Studio Bell, home of the National Music Centre
top.what: Canada's national music museum in East Village: instruments, recording studios and the Canadian Music Hall of Fame.

top.name: Central Library
top.what: The 2018 library in East Village that the CTrain runs underneath, open to everyone: reading rooms, a children's library and a café.

top.name: Stephen Avenue Walk
top.what: The pedestrian street at the centre of downtown, a National Historic Site lined with sandstone buildings from the 1890s, restaurants and patios.

top.name: Plus 15 walkways
top.what: 86 bridges and more than 16 km of enclosed walkways one floor above the street, joining most downtown buildings, 6 am to 9 pm on weekdays.

top.name: Prince's Island Park
top.what: The island park in the Bow River at the north edge of downtown: lawns, the river pathway and the site of the Folk Festival and Canada Day.

top.name: Peace Bridge
top.what: The red footbridge over the Bow, opened in 2012, on the pathway between downtown and Kensington.

top.name: The Confluence Historic Site & Parkland
top.what: Where the Bow and Elbow rivers meet and the North-West Mounted Police built Fort Calgary in 1875: the museum of how the city began, formerly called Fort Calgary.

top.name: Chinatown and the Chinese Cultural Centre
top.what: One of Canada's larger Chinatowns, beside the river: restaurants, shops and the cultural centre with its dome modelled on the Temple of Heaven.

top.name: Contemporary Calgary
top.what: The contemporary art gallery in the former Centennial Planetarium at the west end of downtown.

top.name: Devonian Gardens
top.what: An indoor park on the top floor of the Core shopping centre: a hectare of plants, ponds and a playground, open every day at no charge.

top.name: Wilder Institute / Calgary Zoo
top.what: On St George's Island on the Bow, with the Canadian Wilds, the pandas' former home and the winter Zoolights; its own CTrain station.

top.name: TELUS Spark Science Centre
top.what: The science centre beside the zoo, with a dome theatre and an outdoor park; Adults Only nights once a month.

top.name: Inglewood
top.what: Calgary's first main street (9 Avenue SE, 1875): vintage shops, music venues, breweries and the Inglewood Bird Sanctuary on the river.

top.name: Kensington
top.what: The café and shop district across the Peace Bridge from downtown, one CTrain stop from the core (Sunnyside).

top.name: 17 Avenue SW
top.what: The Beltline's restaurant and patio street, "the Red Mile" when the Flames are in the playoffs.

top.name: Stampede Park, GMC Stadium and the BMO Centre
top.what: Home of the Calgary Stampede each July (more than 1.4 million visits over ten days in 2026), the rodeo grandstand, the BMO Centre convention halls and the Saddledome; the new Scotia Place arena opens in the fall of 2027.

top.name: Heritage Park Historical Village
top.what: Canada's largest living history museum on the Glenmore Reservoir: a steam train, a paddlewheeler, a 1910 town and the Gasoline Alley car museum (open all year); the village opens from May to Thanksgiving and for Christmas weekends.

top.name: Glenmore Reservoir and the Weaselhead
top.what: The city's drinking water reservoir, ringed by a 16 km pathway, with sailing and paddling in summer and the Weaselhead natural area at its west end.

top.name: Fish Creek Provincial Park
top.what: One of the largest urban parks in Canada, 19 km long across the south of the city: paths, Sikome Lake for swimming in summer, and cross-country skiing in winter.

top.name: The Military Museums
top.what: The second-largest military museum in Canada: the Navy, Army and Air Force galleries and the regiments' own museums.

top.name: Nose Hill Park
top.what: Eleven square kilometres of prairie grassland on a hill in the north of the city, with the skyline and the mountains in view from the top.

top.name: Bowness Park
top.what: The riverside park in the northwest: boat rentals and a miniature train in summer, and skating on the lagoon and the river channels in winter.

top.name: WinSport at Canada Olympic Park
top.what: The 1988 Winter Olympics ski jump and bobsleigh site at the west edge of the city: skiing, snowboarding and tubing in winter, mountain biking and the zipline in summer, and public skating indoors all year.

top.name: Olympic Oval
top.what: The 1988 Olympic speed skating oval at the University of Calgary, with public skating sessions on the fast ice.

top.name: Spruce Meadows
top.what: The show jumping grounds at the south edge of the city, with tournaments from June to September (the Masters in September), Cavalry FC soccer from April to October and the Christmas Market in November.

top.name: Calaway Park
top.what: Western Canada's largest outdoor family amusement park, just west of the city on the Trans-Canada Highway, open from May to October.

top.name: Lougheed House
top.what: The 1891 sandstone mansion of Senator James Lougheed in the Beltline, a National Historic Site with gardens and a restaurant.

top.name: Calgary Farmers' Market
top.what: Indoor markets open all year, Thursday to Sunday: the South market on 77 Avenue SE and the West market at Greenbriar.

top.name: The Bow River pathway
top.what: Part of more than 1,000 km of pathways: along the Bow from Bowness to Fish Creek, past downtown, the zoo and Inglewood, with bike share and rentals downtown.

day_trips.name: Banff and Lake Louise
day_trips.what: Banff National Park: the townsite, the gondola, Lake Louise and Moraine Lake (shuttle in summer). A Parks Canada pass is needed to stop in the park.

day_trips.name: Canmore and Kananaskis
day_trips.what: The mountain town of Canmore and Kananaskis Country's trails and lakes; a Kananaskis Conservation Pass is needed to park in Kananaskis.

day_trips.name: Drumheller and the Royal Tyrrell Museum
day_trips.what: The badlands, the hoodoos and Canada's dinosaur museum, 1.5 hours east.

day_trips.name: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump
day_trips.what: The UNESCO World Heritage buffalo jump used by Plains peoples for nearly 6,000 years, near Fort Macleod.

day_trips.name: Waterton Lakes National Park
day_trips.what: Where the prairie meets the mountains at the US border, 3 hours south.

getting_around.title: From the airport
getting_around.what: Calgary International Airport (YYC) is 17 km northeast of downtown. Calgary Transit's Route 300 bus runs between the airport and downtown along Centre Street for the regular adult fare, about 45 to 55 minutes; Route 100 links the airport to the Blue Line CTrain. A taxi to downtown is about $40 to $50 and 25 to 35 minutes; rideshares pick up at the terminal.

getting_around.title: Calgary Transit
getting_around.what: In 2026 an adult single fare is $4.00 (valid 90 minutes), a day pass $12.65, youth $2.65 and children 12 and under ride at no charge; buy fares with Calgary Transit's My Fare on a phone or at CTrain stations. The Red and Blue CTrain lines cross downtown along 7 Avenue, where a trip between the downtown stations costs nothing.

getting_around.title: Finding your way
getting_around.what: Calgary is a grid in four quadrants (NW, NE, SW, SE) split by Centre Street and the Bow River; every address carries its quadrant, and the same street number can exist in all four. Downtown avenues run east-west and streets north-south.

getting_around.title: Downtown on foot
getting_around.what: The Plus 15 walkways (86 bridges, more than 16 km) join most downtown buildings one floor up, open 6 am to 9 pm on weekdays and 9 am to 7 pm at weekends, so a winter day downtown needs no coat between buildings.

getting_around.title: Bikes and pathways
getting_around.what: More than 1,000 km of pathways, with the Bow River pathway through downtown; shared e-bikes and e-scooters are available downtown and in the inner city from spring to fall.

getting_around.title: Driving and the mountains
getting_around.what: Banff is 128 km west on the Trans-Canada Highway, about 90 minutes; winter tires or chains are required on some mountain highways from November to April. A Parks Canada pass is needed inside the national parks and a Kananaskis Conservation Pass to park in Kananaskis.

getting_around.title: Money, tax and tipping
getting_around.what: Alberta has no provincial sales tax: the 5% federal GST applies to most purchases, hotels add a 4% tourism levy (and many a 6% destination marketing fee), and 15 to 20% is the usual tip in restaurants.

getting_around.title: Winter
getting_around.what: December to February are the cold months (the month table shows the averages), with sunny skies most days; a Chinook wind can lift the temperature by 15 to 20 °C in a few hours. Dress in layers; the +15, the CTrain and the malls are warm.

facts.title: The sunniest big city in Canada
facts.what: About 2,396 hours of bright sunshine a year and 333 days with some sun (Environment Canada normals, 1981 to 2010).

facts.title: Chinooks
facts.what: Warm, dry winds off the Rockies that can lift a winter day from −20 °C to above freezing within hours; the Chinook arch of cloud over the mountains announces them.

facts.title: High and dry
facts.what: At 1,045 m above sea level, Calgary is Canada's highest large city; the air is dry, so summer nights cool quickly and the sun is strong.

facts.title: The 1988 Winter Olympics
facts.what: The first Winter Games in Canada, February 13 to 28, 1988; the Olympic Oval, the ski jumps at Canada Olympic Park and the Saddledome are still in use.

facts.title: The Stampede
facts.what: First held in 1912; more than 1.4 million visits over its ten days in 2026.

facts.title: Head offices
facts.what: Calgary has the most head offices per person of any Canadian city and the second-most in total after Toronto, most of them in energy.

facts.title: The Caesar
facts.what: Canada's cocktail was invented at the Calgary Inn in 1969.

facts.title: Parks
facts.what: Fish Creek is one of the largest urban parks in Canada and Nose Hill one of the largest municipal parks; more than 1,000 km of pathways join them.

facts.title: Two rivers
facts.what: The Bow and the Elbow meet at the Confluence, where the city began as a North-West Mounted Police fort in 1875; the Bow is one of the world's best trout rivers inside a city.
